Necessary Sample Size to Reach Desired Power for a Test of the Squared Multiple Correlation in a Multiple Regression Using a Publication Bias and Uncertainty Correction Procedure

Source: R/ss_buc_R2.R
ss_buc_R2.Rd

ss_buc_R2 returns the necessary total sample size to achieve a desired level of statistical power for a test of model \(R^2\) in a planned study using multiple regression, based on information obtained from a previous study. The effect from the previous study can be corrected for publication bias and/or uncertainty to provide a sample size that will achieve more accurate statistical power for a planned study, when compared to approaches that use a sample effect size at face value or rely on sample size only. The bias and uncertainty adjusted previous study noncentrality parameter is also returned, together with the planning effect size, the effect size the plan is built on, as a squared multiple correlation.

Usage

ss_buc_R2(
  F_observed,
  N,
  p,
  alpha_prior = 0.05,
  alpha_planned = 0.05,
  assurance = 0.8,
  desired_power = 0.8,
  random_predictors = FALSE
)

Arguments

F_observed

Observed F value from a previous study used to plan sample size for a planned study.

N

Total sample size of the previous study.

p

Number of predictors; be sure to include any product terms or polynomials that are in the model.

alpha_prior

The significance level \(\alpha\) a prior result had to reach to be published (more generally, to reach you): the correction assumes you see only results with p below alpha_prior. Enter a number above 0 and at most 1. A value of 1, which may also be written "No Publication Filter", means no publication filter: every p value is at most 1, so any result would have been published whatever its p value, there is no publication bias to correct, and only the correction for uncertainty (set by assurance) remains, as for a pilot study. Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017, p. 1552) note that this level, their \(\alpha_P\), can be set equal to 1 when publication bias is thought not to apply. The string is read without regard to case, and the result echoes it as an alpha_prior of 1.

alpha_planned

Alpha level \(\alpha\) assumed for the planned study.

assurance

Desired level of assurance: the long run proportion of planned studies whose statistical power at the true effect reaches or surpasses desired_power, when each is planned from a prior study published under the rule alpha_prior describes. The adjusted noncentrality parameter is the lower limit of a one-sided confidence interval at this level, computed from the publication-truncated distribution of the prior statistic, so assurance = .5 plans from a median unbiased estimate (correcting for publication bias only), a larger value adds the correction for uncertainty, and a value below .5 is not recommended. The term follows Kelley and Maxwell (2003), who used assurance in sample size planning for the probability that a confidence interval will be no wider than desired. With alpha_prior = 1 and assurance = .80 the plan corresponds to safeguard power, which plans for the lower limit of a two-sided 60 percent confidence interval around the prior effect size rather than for the effect size itself (see BUCSS-package for how, and for where the two differ). Enter it as a proportion in (0, 1) or as a percentage greater than 1 (for example, 80 is read as .80); a value of exactly 1 is read as 1 percent. A percentage is echoed in the result's planning-input rows as the coerced proportion (80 is echoed as .80); the same applies to desired_power.

desired_power

Desired level of statistical power for the planned study: the probability that its test rejects the null hypothesis when the effect is present (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027). It must exceed alpha_planned: a test's power is never below its Type I error rate, so a value at or below alpha_planned is not allowable, and the function stops rather than return a plan. Enter it as a proportion in (0, 1) or as a percentage greater than 1; a value of exactly 1 is read as 1 percent (.01), which is then refused unless alpha_planned is below .01.

random_predictors

TRUE if the predictors are sampled along with the outcome, as in most observational research, and FALSE if their values are fixed by design, as in an experiment that assigns them. The default is FALSE, the frame of BUCSS 1.x; see Details. With random predictors (TRUE) the planner uses the exact distribution for sampled predictors that the correlation planner also uses: with one predictor (p = 1) it returns exactly what the correlation planner, ss_buc_correlation, returns. The choice is echoed in the result as a random_predictors row valued 1 (TRUE) or 0 (FALSE) and named in the printed footer.

Value

An object of class bucss_plan: a data.frame with a character term column and a numeric value column, in the same shape as the sibling package DMAR's planners. The design results come first: the necessary total sample size for the planned study, named for its unit (necessary_n_per_group, necessary_n_per_cell, or necessary_N); for the per-group and per-cell designs, total_N, the implied total sample size; actual_power, the power of the plan returned, that is, of the returned sample size at the returned noncentrality parameter (see Details); ncp_adjusted, the publication bias and uncertainty adjusted prior study noncentrality parameter, on the scale of the F statistic at the prior study's sample size; and the planning effect size, R2_planning, the population squared multiple correlation, \(\lambda/(\lambda + N)\), where \(\lambda\) is ncp_adjusted and N the prior sample size; the planned study's power is computed from it at the planned sample size, in the frame random_predictors names (with sampled predictors the power statement that follows is in that frame).

A planning effect size (the row whose name ends in _planning) is an adjusted effect size: the value, in the design's usual effect size metric, used to plan the sample size given the situation at hand (the prior study's result, the publication bias assumed through alpha_prior, and the uncertainty allowed for through assurance). It is ncp_adjusted restated in that metric and is what the plan is built on, not an estimate of the population effect to report: above an assurance of .5 it is deliberately conservative (a lower confidence limit), and at .5 it is the median unbiased estimate. Because it restates ncp_adjusted, actual_power is the ordinary power of a study of the returned sample size when the population effect is the planning effect size.

Rows echoing the planning inputs follow the design results, so the assumptions travel with the result. The design, the unit the sample size is counted in, the largest assurance this prior can support (the assurance ceiling), and the planned test's degrees of freedom (df_effect, and df_error where the test has a denominator) travel on attributes. print.bucss_plan shows the design, for the regression planners the predictor frame, the unit, and the ceiling beneath the table; tidy() and glance() give the compact and wide views, the latter with every attribute as a column.

Details

Researchers often use the sample effect size from a prior study as an estimate of the likely size of an expected future effect in sample size planning. However, sample effect size estimates should not usually be used at face value to plan sample size, due to both publication bias and uncertainty.

The approach implemented in ss_buc_R2 uses the observed F value and sample size from a previous study to correct the noncentrality parameter associated with the effect of interest for publication bias and/or uncertainty. This new estimated noncentrality parameter is then used to calculate the necessary total sample size to achieve the desired level of power in the planned study.

Fixed or random predictors. Whether the predictors' values are fixed by design, as in an experiment in which the researcher sets them, or sampled along with the outcome, as in most observational research, changes neither the estimates nor the distribution of the test statistic when every coefficient is zero, but it does change the statistic's distribution, and so the power, when they are not all zero (Sampson, 1974; Gatsonis & Sampson, 1989; Kelley & Maxwell, 2003). With random_predictors = FALSE, the default, the prior study's statistic and the planned study's power come from the noncentral F distribution, which is exact when the predictor values are fixed; this is the frame of BUCSS 1.x and of Anderson (2021). With random_predictors = TRUE the noncentrality parameter is itself random: it is proportional to the predictors' sampled spread, a chi square variable on N - 1 degrees of freedom, so the statistic follows a chi square mixture of noncentral F distributions, which is more dispersed. This is the exact distribution of the squared multiple correlation when the predictors are sampled (the general sampling distribution of the multiple correlation coefficient; Fisher, 1928), the one for which Gatsonis and Sampson (1989) give exact power and sample size calculations. The mixture has an exact closed form (the Poisson weights of the noncentral F become negative binomial weights), used for both the correction and the planned study's power. It is exact when the predictors are multivariate normal. In observational research in the behavioral sciences the predictors are typically random (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003), and random_predictors = TRUE is then the frame to plan in.

Treating sampled predictors as fixed overstates the planned study's power, by about 1/n for a plan of n participants with one predictor, 1.2/n with three, and 1.4/n with eight to ten (.010 to .014 at n = 100, and .05 to .06 at n = 20), so the assurance the plans deliver falls a little short of the requested assurance. The delivered assurance is what assurance promises: the proportion of plans, each made from its own published prior study, whose power at the true effect reaches desired_power, counting a refusal to plan as meeting the target. In simulations with three multivariate normal predictors, an assurance of .80, and prior studies with power .3 to .8 at the true effect, the fixed frame delivered about .76 to .80 from prior studies of 30 to 40, the lower values from better powered prior studies, and .79 to .80 from prior studies of 100 to 300; random_predictors = TRUE delivered .79 to .82 in the same configurations. The random-predictor plan is usually a few participants larger; close to the assurance ceiling, where plans run to thousands, it can be a few percent smaller. The largest assurance a prior result can support is the same in both frames, because at a zero effect both are the central F distribution. With one predictor and random_predictors = TRUE this function returns exactly what ss_buc_correlation returns for the same prior t (the square root of F_observed) and N (the same sample size, power, noncentrality parameter, and ceiling, with the planning effect size stated as \(R^2\), the square of the correlation), for any prior N of at least 4 (the correlation planner's minimum).

The approach uses a likelihood function of a truncated noncentral F distribution, where the truncation occurs due to small effect sizes being unobserved due to publication bias. The numerator of the likelihood function is the density of a noncentral F distribution (with random_predictors = TRUE, of the mixture described above). The denominator is the power of the test, which serves to truncate the distribution. Thus, the ratio of the numerator and the denominator is a truncated noncentral F distribution. (See Taylor & Muller, 1996, Equation 2.1; Anderson, Kelley, & Maxwell, 2017, Equation 3; and Anderson & Maxwell, 2017, for more details.)

Assurance is the proportion of times that power will be at or above the desired level, if the experiment were to be reproduced many times. For example, assurance = .5 means that power will be above the desired level half of the time, but below the desired level the other half of the time. Selecting assurance = .5 (selecting the noncentrality parameter at the 50th percentile of the likelihood distribution) results in a median unbiased estimate of the population noncentrality parameter and does not correct for uncertainty. In order to correct for uncertainty, assurance > .5 can be selected, which corresponds to selecting the noncentrality parameter associated with the (1 - assurance) quantile of the likelihood distribution.

alpha_prior is the significance level a prior result had to reach to be published: the correction assumes that only results with p values below alpha_prior reach the literature, and so reach you. Different \(\alpha\) levels represent differing amounts of publication bias. For example, setting alpha_prior = .20 assumes that studies with p values less than .20 are published, whereas those with larger p values are not, which reflects less severe publication bias than the default of .05. If the previous study of interest has not been subjected to publication bias (e.g., a pilot study), set alpha_prior = 1, which may also be written alpha_prior = "No Publication Filter"; Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017, p. 1552) note that it can be set equal to 1 when publication bias is thought not to apply. Because no p value exceeds 1, this means no publication filter at all: any result would have been published whatever its p value, so there is no publication bias to correct, and only the correction for uncertainty, set by assurance, remains.

In some cases, the corrected noncentrality parameter for a given level of assurance will be estimated to be zero. This is an indication that, at the desired level of assurance, the previous study's effect cannot be accurately estimated due to high levels of uncertainty and bias. When this happens, subsequent sample size planning is not possible with the chosen specifications, and the function stops with an informative error rather than returning a result. The error reports the largest assurance the prior result can support, which is \(1 - p/\alpha\), where p is the prior study's p value and \(\alpha\) is alpha_prior; at any higher assurance the corrected noncentrality parameter is driven to zero. Two remedies are available. First, users can select a lower value of assurance (e.g., .8 instead of .95), at or below the reported ceiling. Second, users can reduce the influence of publication bias by setting alpha_prior at a value greater than .05, which raises the ceiling. Note that alpha_prior is not a property of the prior study, which is fixed, but the analyst's assumption about the publication threshold its literature faced. When the ceiling is at or below the recommended floor of .5, lowering assurance cannot help and alpha_prior is the only remaining lever. It is possible to correct for uncertainty only by setting alpha_prior = 1 and choosing the desired level of assurance. We encourage users to make the adjustments as minimal as possible.

The returned actual_power is the statistical power of the plan this function reports: the power of a study of the returned sample size when the effect is the returned bias and uncertainty adjusted noncentrality parameter. Because a sample size must be a whole number, actual_power is never below the desired_power that was requested and is usually a little above it.

The search for the planned sample size starts at p + 3, the smallest total that leaves the planned study two error degrees of freedom (as in BUCSS 1.x), so no plan is smaller than that, even when the prior effect is so large that a smaller study would already reach the desired power. A plan at this floor signals a very large prior effect, not a recommended design.

Examples

result <- ss_buc_R2(F_observed = 5, N = 150, p = 4, alpha_prior = .05,
  alpha_planned = .05, assurance = .80, desired_power = .80)
result
#>  term              value 
#>  necessary_N       234   
#>  actual_power      0.8   
#>  ncp_adjusted      7.82  
#>  R2_planning       0.0495
#>  F_observed        5     
#>  N                 150   
#>  p                 4     
#>  random_predictors 0     
#>  alpha_prior       0.05  
#>  alpha_planned     0.05  
#>  assurance         0.8   
#>  desired_power     0.8   
#> 
#> Design: Multiple regression: omnibus test of model R2
#> Predictors: fixed by design
#> Sample size unit: total
#> Largest supportable assurance: .98

# Predictors sampled along with the outcome, as in most observational
# research:
ss_buc_R2(F_observed = 5, N = 150, p = 4, random_predictors = TRUE)
#>  term              value 
#>  necessary_N       239   
#>  actual_power      0.801 
#>  ncp_adjusted      7.76  
#>  R2_planning       0.0492
#>  F_observed        5     
#>  N                 150   
#>  p                 4     
#>  random_predictors 1     
#>  alpha_prior       0.05  
#>  alpha_planned     0.05  
#>  assurance         0.8   
#>  desired_power     0.8   
#> 
#> Design: Multiple regression: omnibus test of model R2
#> Predictors: random (sampled along with the outcome)
#> Sample size unit: total
#> Largest supportable assurance: .98

# Requesting more assurance than the prior result can support stops with an
# informative error naming the largest workable assurance (here near .98):
try(ss_buc_R2(F_observed = 5, N = 150, p = 4, assurance = .99))
#> Error : Sample size planning is not possible with these settings. After correcting the prior study's effect for publication bias and uncertainty at the requested level of assurance, the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, which means there is not enough information in the prior result to plan the sample size as desired. With this prior result and 'alpha_prior', the largest 'assurance' that still yields a usable plan is about .98; re-run with 'assurance' at or below that value, or raise 'alpha_prior' to lift the ceiling. Re-running at a lower 'assurance' is not free: the plan it returns carries that lower assurance, not the one you first asked for, so the long run proportion of replications reaching your target power falls accordingly. 'alpha_prior' does not change the prior study, which is what it is; it is your assumption about the publication threshold the study's literature faced, so raising it toward 1 assumes less publication bias to undo (for example, 'alpha_prior = .10' assumes the literature's journals would have published a result significant at the .10 level, a more lenient policy than .05, and 'alpha_prior = 1' assumes no publication bias at all). See Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017) and Anderson and Kelley (2024).
